#4859. Latest Canadian budget packs funding for 55,000 new EV chargers

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 new EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of new public EV charging stations.

“The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”

The rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, new data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

I sincerely hope this promotes the idea of installing fast chargers along routes with lower populations. I live in Ottawa, driving to my home town in northern Ontario has pretty much a single fast charger, a Tesla one with short cables at the mid point about 2.25h in. 6 stalls. If that goes down, there is nothing for about 400km of a decent charging speed. They need to have alternatives to Tesla (I've been very reliant on Tesla stations and don't own a Tesla) and more stations in between the current Tesla stations. Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

If Washington doesn’t see that for, “Go pound sand, eh?” that it is, then it’s truly lost the plot – but even if the “blue wave” last week was enough to shake a little sense into the folks running the show, it may already be too late to patch things up.

#4858. 9-foot-tall Game Boy Color plays all the classics

Published Nov 11, 2026 8:53 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

A pair of California-based engineers have built what they say may be the largest Game Boy Color ever. Standing more than nine feet and weighing around 300 pounds, the Pokémon-yellow goliath requires a U-Haul to transport and took over 1,500 collective hours in a makerspace to create. And it isn’t just for show. The giant handheld plays real Game Boy games, thanks to a pixel-perfect display scaled up from the original and software written from scratch. The designers even fabricated an assortment of to-scale accessories, including game cartridges, a cable link, and AA batteries.

The console has already appeared at several maker events, where eager kids have punched and kicked its chunky buttons. It has also prompted plenty of older millennials, in person and online, to reminisce about simpler days. Build videos posted across social media have racked up hundreds of thousands of views. But for co-creator Paige Powell, a veteran prop designer and mechanical engineer, the giant Game Boy also represents something more special: a labor of love and a chance to inspire young girls to start building things themselves.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

“It [has] felt very weird to me in a very male-dominated world to build something behind the scenes and then give it to [a] guy who then takes credit,” Powell tells Popular Science. “I want people to see women making stuff!”

The giant GameBoy is the joint effort of Powell (@whats_paige_making on Instagram) and engineer Nick Alvarez (@nickbuildstuff on Instagram). Powell has a long track record of building props and sets for the YouTube channel Mega Builds and the immersive art company Meow Wolf. Alvarez, meanwhile, specializes in PCB (printed circuit board) design and spent seven years as a full-time engineering manager at an aerospace defense company.

The two crossed paths while working at the Davis makerspace, just west of Sacramento. Alvarez was building a large LED wall (the kind used for screens at sports arenas) and wanted to hook up Nintendo controllers so it could play games. Piggybacking off of that, Powell proposed taking the idea a step further: a giant playable Game Boy. From there, it only made sense to try and make the world’s largest. That sent them down a rabbit hole that would consume a sizable chunk of their lives (and finances) over the months to follow.

A quick bit of research revealed they weren’t the first one with this idea. Guinness World Records actually has an official entry for the Largest Game Boy Color, an accolade claimed in 2022 by a YouTuber named Jake Carlini. His version measured in at seven feet tall. But calling that one a real Game Boy is quite a stretch. It was really little more than a few pieces of vaguely detailed plywood. Alvarez and Powell realized there was an opportunity, not just to break the record, but to build something far more ambitious.

“It [the Carlini model] was just kind of [a] slapstick way of putting it together, and we were like, ‘dude, what is this?’ Alvarez says. ”We can do something actually amazing with our background and our skillset.”

From the outset, the duo gave themselves a set of constraints to build around. Their Game Boy had to be to scale to the original and functional as a game console. They also committed to making the screen pixel perfect to the 1998 original.

“Everything was built around the constraint of what the screen was going to be,” Powell says.

Fortunately, they had some help along the way. When they told Tim Keller, the head of the Davis makerspace, about the project, he agreed to let them set up shop and use the space’s CNC mills, 3D printers, laser cutters, and other equipment.

Meet the college student crafting electric guitars from scratch

This guy crammed a laptop into an Altoids tin

Clever kid builds phone charger powered by pet hamster

Teen brothers build a Disney-inspired ride in family basement

In Vermont, one man is bringing pay phones back to life

With goals set and tools secured, the pair then created a 3D model of their scaled-up Game Boy, starting with a smaller (though still shockingly large) 5.7-foot version. Powell quickly realized that the toughest part to fabricate wasn’t actually the console’s iconic front, but rather its geometrically odd-shaped back shell. The top of the backside starts out flat but then bulges out into a sloped shape toward the bottom where a person would hold it in their palm. The cartridge slot where the game slides into also juts out from the back, adding even more complexity

Once the 3D model was complete, Powell began building the physical body, made mostly of plywood shaped on the CNC machine, an automated manufacturing device that reads computer code and uses that to control cutting machines like mills, lathes, and lasers. CNC machines are indispensable tools in many makers’ arsenals. But a project like this requires adaptability. Partway through, Powell says, she realized the CNC machine wasn’t all that well suited to making square cuts, which meant the final product would need more hand carpentry than initially planned.

Meanwhile, Alvarez was hard at work perfecting the display and electronics under the hood (or, in this case, the shell). He built the screen from a series of HUB75 LED panels, the kind commonly used in large digital signs. The trick was getting his massive DIY display to scale up accurately from the original GameBoy’s 160-by-144 pixel screen. He also used a small microcontroller (essentially a tiny computer assigned to a specific task) to map all of the device’s buttons and switches.

When the giant Game Boy plays games, it’s running them on a specialized emulator rather than the physical game cartridge that gets slotted into the device. The emulator is a piece of software that imitates a Game Boy. Emulators are common these days and are what let hobbyists play old Nintendo games on smartphones.

The to-scale cartridges Powell and Alvarez fabricated are really more for show. That means, theoretically, their device can run any Game Boy game. Alvarez says he even built in a feature that cycles to a different game each time the power is switched on. So far, the pair have posted videos of the device playing Pokémon and Donkey Kong. Alvarez even watched The Odyssey on it.

Powell and Alvarez have shown off their creations at two events so far: Open Sauce in 2026 and the Bay Area Maker Fair in Vallejo, California. Getting the Game Boys there was a task in itself. The larger of the two (around 300 pounds) required a large U-Haul and four people just to load it. Once unloaded, they faced a more daunting challenge: the wrath of children. Drawn in by the device’s giant buttons, kids at the events let loose.

“Kids were coming up and karate-kicking them, and I was just like, ‘Oh my God, man,’” Powell says.

Alvarez concurs. “They were punching the crap out of the buttons.”

In a testament to its build quality, the giant Game Boy withstood the onslaught of toddler haymakers. Those who weren’t assailing the device were often absorbing an emotional gut punch of their own. Both in person and online, fans told Powell and Alvarez how the build brought back childhood memories. One commenter recalled how seeing it reminded them of a time at a school when a bully stole their beloved Game Boy. Decades later, he said, he’s still mad.

Looking ahead, Powell and Alvarez hope to find their creation a new home where it can be on display and accessible to the public. They’d like to recoup some of the money they’ve poured into it, but Powell also expressed some wariness of it winding up locked away in some buyer’s private collection. Ideally, she says, it would land in a museum of some kind, where it could inspire the next generation of budding makers.

#4857. With Age Comes a Unique Ability to Harness the Power of AI

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Co-authored by George S. Everly, Jr., PhD, MA, ABPP, and Barry McGovern, Solutions Engineer, JBS International

Today, November 19, 2026, is an important day in the world of artificial intelligence (AI). Anthropic, a major artificial intelligence company, is beginning to sell ownership shares of stock in the company to the public. At the same time, Anthropic’s founder, Dario Amodei, issued a warning. He cautioned that AI is developing more rapidly than expected, especially through the process of recursive self-improvement, which allows the programs to improve themselves without human guidance.

We often look to younger generations when it comes to guidance regarding AI. Perhaps surprisingly, older generations may have much to offer in managing and directing AI, especially at the level of personal use. Decades of lived experience, pattern recognition, and knowing how to ask the right questions allow older generations to harness the power of AI through the process of “prompt engineering” in a way that is more mature and experience-informed than it is for younger generations.

On average, older adults (age 50 or older) are more skeptical of artificial intelligence (AI), less trusting of its responses to questions, and less likely to use it than younger adults. While caution is warranted, older adults possess a hidden “superpower” in the form of prompt engineering based upon lived experience that, at least at this point, allows them to become active managers of AI rather than non-critical users, overly cautious passive recipients, or worse yet, non-participants. Ironically, this “superpower” is more prevalent in older adults than younger adults and may increase to some degree with age.

For adults aged 18-40, the use of AI is likely 70 percent or higher. However, survey research conducted by AARP (AARP, September 23, 2025) found that familiarity with and use of AI decrease with age. About 47 percent of adults in their 50s reported knowing about and using AI, compared with 25 percent of those over 70.

As described in a previous post, AI may encourage passive, non-critical consumption of information. The risks of such passive consumption have yet to be fully determined, but AI may lead to the inhibition of critical thinking and the creation of a functional dependence. A recent TV commercial showed a character gleefully stating that she has difficulty thinking without AI. It is this very passivity that increases the risk of an untethered AI.

Younger users may seem to treat AI like an answer machine because they don't yet have the foundational knowledge to critically assess the validity of the information provided. Older adults, by contrast, have a built-in "lie-detector” from decades of career and life experience—in short, they know what a valid answer is supposed to look like and may be better positioned than younger adults to ask follow-up questions that can challenge AI.

Francis Bacon once noted, “If a man will begin with certainties, he shall end in doubts; but if he will be content to begin with doubts, he shall end in certainties.” So far, the errors or “overzealousness” exhibited by AI appear to be related to the questions asked of it. The more vague or less structured the questions, and the more repetitive the questions posed to AI, the greater its tendency to try to anticipate the desired answer and to “please” the questioner by “hallucinating” and creating spurious evidence to support the desired conclusions even though incorrect. In addition, AI does not possess the ability to independently assess the validity of the data it retrieves nor its recombinant output. As such, it may provide misleading or erroneous information.

The aging process is often accompanied by the accumulation of insights, knowledge, and informative experiences. These attributes may reveal themselves as the “superpower” ability to formulate specific, targeted questions. Rather than fostering passive consumption, knowledge and experience can foster informed, active consumption. It fosters the potential for a complementary, if not synergistic, relationship with AI wherein the person formulates knowledge- and experience-informed questions that not only target the efforts of AI but can serve as a series of checks and balances through AI’s recombinant efforts to provide answers.

For instance, a younger, less experienced person might ask AI, "Write me a business plan" (passive, vague), while a 60-year-old might ask, "Construct a business plan that overcomes these three most common reasons new tech companies fail" (experience-driven, targeted). Or, the less experienced consultant might ask AI, “Write an independent contractor’s agreement” (vague, too general), as opposed to “Create an independent contractor’s agreement that ensures the ownership of my pre-existing intellectual property does not transfer as a work for hire” (very specific, anticipating potential confusion over ownership).

Socrates believed the highest form of wisdom arose from introspection and self-reflection. Just as he used questions to challenge his students to provide the best answers to the most pressing questions of his day, perhaps we can harness questions in the Socratic method to guide AI to provide us with the answers to the most pressing questions of our day.

#4855. Police charge another Tesla driver caught asleep in rush hour as cases pile up

A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared shows a new-generation Model Y in traffic.

The charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”

According to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

Careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:

This isn’t new in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

The U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

And in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

Waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

Tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

Since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual says about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”

In other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

The penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

And Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk said in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

The Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

We’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

People have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

But police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

The fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

#4853. Underwater internet cables can help save endangered whales

Published Nov 11, 2026 12:01 PM EST

The world’s oceans are crisscrossed by thousands of miles of deep sea fiber-optic cables. This immense infrastructure is the foundation for much of the planet’s international power transmission and telecommunications, but marine biologists say the lines can provide an unexpected conservation benefit. With a bit of creative retooling, the ocean cables can also function as surprisingly good microphones for monitoring endangered whale populations.

“This is truly exciting, as this technology enables real-time data access over tens of [miles], and from land,” said Cornell University bioacoustics researcher Léa Bouffaut.

The latest advancements were recently detailed in the journal Methods in Ecology and Evolution, and build on Bouffaut’s previous work. In 2022, her team became the first researchers to demonstrate fiber-optic cable monitoring of blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) and fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus). The two species are respectively the largest and second-largest cetaceans, which also means they generate loud, ultra-low frequency vocalizations under 100 hertz. To record their calls, Bouffaut and colleagues utilized a system called distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). The technique works by sending laser pulses through deep sea cables using specialized equipment, which researchers then analyze for miniscule sonic alterations caused by environmental sound waves. After pinpointing blue and fin whale communications, researchers then used the cables’ positions to map the marine mammals’ movements and population distribution.

Following her initial demonstrations, Bouffaut was curious if DAS could also work for other baleen whale species. The odds necessarily weren’t in her team’s favor—smaller species like the bowhead whale (Balaena mysticetus) and critically endangered North Atlantic right whale (Eubalaena glacialis) issue calls at much higher frequencies between about 150 and 300 hertz. Their vocalizations are also less intense and travel shorter distances, making them even more difficult to parse in DAS data.

In the spring, Bouffaut traveled to the town of Utqiaġvik on Alaska’s North Slope to collaborate with the local Indigenous Iñupiat community of whalers. She also partnered with Arctic broadband company Quintillion, who provided access to one of their own deep sea telecommunications cables. Amid terabytes of DAS recordings, Bouffaut eventually achieved another first in her field. She became the first person to confirm bowhead whale vocalizations by harnessing fiber-optic cables.

“Being able to detect bowhead whales on a telecommunication cable is the proof of concept we need to show that DAS can be used to monitor all baleen whales,” explained Bouffaut.

Although the new strategy isn’t sensitive enough to replace dedicated ocean monitoring using underwater microphone arrays, Bouffaut and her colleagues believe DAS could become an invaluable additional tool. It also showcases a way to convert existing infrastructures into multi-use systems.

“The review is also a call to action for scientists, industry partners and regulators to collaborate,” said Bouffaut. “We now have the technical blueprint to turn global undersea infrastructure into a global network for ocean conservation.”

#4852. Volkswagen’s new electric SUV is taking over where the ID.4 left off

Volkswagen is turning one of its best-selling nameplates into an electric SUV. The new ID. Tiguan is now rolling off the assembly line and will replace the ID.4 in 2027.

The ID.4 and ID.5 are on the way out, and the new ID. Tiguan will replace them in Volkswagen’s EV lineup next year.

Following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, which are now on sale in Europe, the ID. Tiguan is the next model to go on sale as a “True Volkswagen,” as the company calls it.

The new electric SUV adopts Volkswagen’s best-selling nameplate, the Tiguan, as part of its shift away from the numerical system used on the outgoing ID.4 and ID.5.

Volkswagen announced on Thursday that series production of the electric ID. Tiguan has now begun at its Embden Plant in Germany.

“The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars,” VW Brand CEO Thomas Shafer said last month after unveiling the new SUV. He added that “The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together.”

The ID. Tiguan will be a step change from its predecessors, the ID.4 and ID.5, featuring Volkswagen’s “Pure Positive” design language, which includes an overhauled interior and exterior design and updated tech.

Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan’s “hallmark feature” is the completely redesigned exterior. The new design remains closer to the gas-powered Tiguan, with a boxy, traditional SUV look.

Unlike the ID.4’s aerodynamic design, the new ID. Tiguan features a wide, chunky front end and traditional pull-style door handles instead of the flush ones.

In Volkswagen’s words, the new ID. Tiguan electric SUV “looks like a vehicle from the premium segment.”

Inside, the updates are just as evident. The overhauled interior features Volkswagen’s new infotainment setup, including a 10″ Digital Cockpit and a 15″ center display. There’s also an optional 12″ passenger screen available.

To spark a bit of nostalgia, VW added a fun new Retro Mode feature that transforms the Digital Cockpit and center display to mimic the style of iconic models like the first-generation Golf.

The new Volkswagen ID. Tiguan will be available with two battery packs and three performance levels:

Depending on the configuration, the ID. Tiguan offers a “new benchmark” for Volkswagen’s electric SUVs in Europe with a WLTP range of up to 377 miles (607 km).

Volkswagen opened orders for the ID. Tiguan in Germany and a few other European markets in October, starting at €42,695 ($47,800). It’s available in three trims: Trend, Life, and Style.

After it launches in Europe through early 2027, Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan will go on sale in North America to replace the ID.4.

Apparently, the new ID Tiguan has a slightly better Cx (Drag Coefficient) at 0.26 versus 0.28 on first gen ID4 and 0.27 on 2nd gen. According to VW, it’s achieved using front air curtains, a minimal air intake, an enclosed underbody, and a longer roof spoiler.

Volkswagen said prices and other details will come in “due course.” The current VW ID.4 uses an 82 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 291 miles in the RWD version. The AWD model offers around 263 miles.

Since the European model offers close to 25 miles (40 km) more WLTP range than the outgoing ID.4, the ID. Tiguan is expected to offer over 300 miles on the EPA scale.

Official US prices have not yet been announced. The outgoing ID.4 has a starting MSRP of about $45,000, so the ID. Tiguan will likely be priced similarly.

#4851. Chunky mama bear wins 2026 Nope award for quick retreat from bigger rival

Published Nov 11, 2026 1:12 PM EST

Despite both species being bears, black bears (Ursus americanus) typically won’t go to areas that brown bears (Ursus arctos) frequent. For one, brown bears are bigger, at 600 to 900 pounds to the black bear’s average of 90 to 500 pounds.

Despite her large stature (and award-winning butt), a mother bear in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska named Volverine instantly turned around when she noticed a female brown bear named Bullseye standing right behind her. The U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded her the 2026 Nope Award for her quick turn away from Bullseye.

“It took a minute for Volverine to notice Bullseye the brown bear standing right behind her, but when she saw, she said, ‘Nope!’” the rangers write.

Bullseye is a five-year-old brown bear who is known for dark circles around her eyes, and dark brown fur mixed into her blonde coat. And if you are keeping score at home, this is Volverine’s second award this season. She also won the 2026 Big & Beautiful Award for her beautiful bulky body.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for tourists on Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like Volverine and eight brown bears like Bullseye. Similar to  their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their antics.

#4849. How to Prevent Arguments at Thanksgiving Dinner

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Gary Drevitch

The days leading up to Thanksgiving can feel like a whirlwind. Between figuring out who’s bringing what and dodging holiday traffic, nerves can wear thin before the first guest arrives. The extra leaf has to be wrestled out of the closet to stretch the table a little longer, and someone has been up since dawn coaxing the turkey toward golden. By the time everyone sits down, the coats are piled high on a bed down the hall and someone is sneaking a roll before grace. Then, somewhere between the first helping and the pie, a loaded remark cuts across the table and the tension becomes palpable. We spend weeks preparing the meal, yet the conversations shared over it rarely receive the same forethought.

Over the years, journalists have asked me how to keep Thanksgiving conversations from boiling over, and I always say we can’t control what others say or do, but we can choose how we respond. The key is remembering the person across the table matters more than proving a point.

Before the gathering, it helps to take inventory of ourselves. I think of it like packing for a trip somewhere new. We check the forecast and pack for the weather we expect, knowing the skies can still shift once we land. In the same way, we can reflect on which topics might feel sensitive this year.

If some relatives tend to bring up challenging subjects, a quick heads-up can make those conversations easier to navigate. We might say, “I’ve been looking forward to being together, and it would mean a lot if we could keep things lighter this year.” Sharing this means everyone can arrive on the same page and enjoy one another’s company.

Thanksgiving conversations have a way of wandering into topics no one meant to open. A comment lands the wrong way and suddenly we’re deciding whether to let it go or respond. A racing heart can be a cue to take a breath and pause. In that pause, we can ask ourselves three questions:

These questions can help us decide how, if at all, to engage. If the answer to any of them is no, we can steer the conversation toward common ground. We don’t have to follow every conversation into the weeds. Sometimes the kindest thing we can do for a conversation is to decide not to have it.

At the same time, steering clear of hard topics isn’t always the answer. A difficult conversation doesn’t have to strain our relationships. Research on Thanksgiving discussions suggests that college students whose families encouraged open conversation reported more positive effects on family closeness and less stress afterward.

A disagreement does not have to become an argument. Much depends on whether we are trying to prove a point or to understand someone. Scholarship on serial arguments indicates that people often care more about working things out together than gaining the upper hand. Arguments tend to take hold once difference feels like a threat, pulling us into an either/or mindset where one view must prevail over the other. To stay on the side of understanding, we can ask ourselves, “How can I express my views while still showing respect and valuing this person?” If a conversation feels uncomfortable, we might say, “I hear you, and I hold a different perspective.” Sentiments like these help others feel heard, even when we see things differently.

Of course, it wouldn’t be Thanksgiving without someone bringing up that topic—the one half the family has been hoping to avoid. We try to change the subject, and for a few minutes the conversation moves on to football and Black Friday deals. Then, just as everyone relaxes, that same relative finds a way back to the topic. It’s understandable to feel frustrated, yet shutting down the conversation can create more distance. After all, this is someone who matters to us, and there may be something more going on beneath the surface.

Difficult conversations can be complex webs of unspoken needs and hidden emotions. Maybe our relative is trying to make sense of something they’re going through, or looking for connection without knowing how to express that need. They may feel anxious or unheard. Or, there may be reasons we haven’t considered at all.

Without fully knowing the reason, some thoughtfulness can go a long way. It’s worth considering the experiences that may be influencing their viewpoint. Stepping into another’s shoes, even for a moment, can foster understanding and empathy. Offered sincerely, an affirmation such as “I can tell how much you care about this” conveys they are seen and heard, which can change the tone of the whole conversation.

Other times, we watch from the sidelines as two relatives barrel toward an argument we all saw coming. Family arguments often gain momentum through the quick volley of replies, each one arriving a little faster and a little louder than the last. Before long, the momentum takes over in ways the original comment never would have on its own.

In situations like these, we can interrupt the pace, not the people. A calm invitation such as “This feels a little tense. Maybe we can pause this for now” can slow things down, and families tend to respond more openly to understanding than to judgment. Asking a relative to help carry dishes to the kitchen or check on the pie breaks the rhythm without putting anyone on the spot, giving each person a graceful way to step back with their dignity intact. The goal isn’t to referee or get everyone to agree, but to give the whole table a chance to reset.

Keeping the peace at Thanksgiving doesn’t require everyone to share the same point of view, and understanding someone else’s doesn’t mean giving up our own. We can, however, choose how we treat one another, even when we disagree.

Bevan, J. L. (2010). Serial argument goals and conflict strategies: A comparison between romantic partners and family members. Communication Reports, 23(1), 52–64. doi.org/10.1080/08934211003598734

Johnson, A. J., Bostwick, E. N., & Cionea, I. A. (2019). Talking turkey: Effects of family discussions about the 2016 election over the Thanksgiving holiday. Journal of Family Communication, 19(1), 63–76. doi.org/10.1080/15267431.2018.1543688

#4847. Children made some of the Middle East’s oldest known clay figures

Published Nov 11, 2026 2:00 PM EST

About 10,000 years ago, a Neolithic culture in the southern Levant known as the Natufians became some of the first nomadic hunter-gatherers to transition towards agriculture. But even before this monumental lifestyle shift, members of the prehistoric community were already crafting symbolic figures from clay. What’s more, archaeologists say more than 150 recently discovered artifacts dating back 11,500 to 15,000 years ago are likely the earliest examples of their kind ever found in the Middle East. Their findings, published today in the journal PLOS One, suggest that even children sometimes had a role in creating these miniatures.

The Natufians lived in what is now known as the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE. Pre-agrarian and semi-sedentary, the culture likely preceded the region’s first permanent Neolithic settlements. Although archaeologists previously located small figurines linked to the Natufians made from rocks and bones, these clay artifacts have larger implications. Crafting items from preexisting hard materials typically relies on intentionally shaping through processes like breaking, sanding, or whittling. The existence of clay items suggests that the Natufians didn’t just express themselves artistically and symbolically. They did so through materials that required additional steps like baking and hardening.

“This shift required diverse tools, skills, and knowledge, different from those needed for the manipulation of stone and bone,” the study’s authors wrote.

The figurines found at sites across present-day Israel include depictions of animals like birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as both male and female individuals. Some of the pieces exhibit traces of pigment and other dyes, while others still feature ancient fingerprints of the artists themselves. Further examinations of these indentations shows that clay sculpting was an intergenerational craft, with both children and adults taking part in the activity.

“Thousands of years before agriculture and pottery emerged, people were already using clay to create figures, as part of their beliefs and knowledge of the natural world,” Laurent Davin, a study co-author and archaeologist at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said in a statement. “What is particularly fascinating is the evidence that children were involved in making these objects, suggesting that creativity and cultural knowledge were shared across generations.”

#4846. Fera Fruit Oil Claims It’s Healthier Than Even Avocado Oil. Should You Make the Switch?

EREWHON, EVERYONE’S FAVORITE love-to-hate overpriced supermarket chain made news recently for switching up their oils. Yes, the certified organic grocer announced that it's no longer using avocado oil to fry its cafe food. Instead, all 15 locations are switching to certified organic fera fruit oil.

Erewhon isn’t the only company hawking fera fruit oil as a way to further health-ify their vegan buffalo cauliflower and turmeric chicken tenders. Since launching in April 2026, the oil is now in more than 800 grocers, restaurants, wellness clubs, and luxury hotels like Mezeh Mediterranean Grill and Wynn Las Vegas.

Fera fruit oil may sound exotic and healthy (it’s made from fruit?), but as a registered dietitian, I'm not one for assumptions when it comes to food. Especially when it coincides with the peak of seed-oil fear-messaging. Keep reading to learn what this new-to-the-scene frying oil is and if it's really worth the hype.

FERA FRUIT OIL is basically palm oil. The company behind it, Zero Acre Farms, trademarked the name “fera fruit oil” for high oleic palm oil, a type of palm oil that's produced by pressing the fruit of a hybrid palm tree called Oleifera × Guineensis (OxG for short).

The hybrid plant was originally planted by farmers to reduce bud rot, a disease that notoriously destroys palm crops. A happy side effect was that the oil also ended up having higher oleic acid content, the same heart-healthy monounsaturated fat found in avocado and olive oil.

TRADITIONALLY GROWN PALM has a problematic history of deforestation, but according to Zero Acre Farms, fera fruit oil is a perennial crop that requires just 0.3 acres to produce a ton of oil, using 15 to 20 times less land than soybean or canola oil.

Of course, Zero Acre Farms’ website doesn't cite sources for these numbers, so I did my own digging. Independent research suggests traditional palm yields 3.3 tons per hectare, which is impressive compared to soybean, canola, and sunflower, which collectively produce 0.6 tons per hectare. But OxG palm yields about 1 ton less than traditional palm, which means the demonized seed oils use 3 to 4 times more land, not 15 to 20 times. So the claims seem a bit sensationalized at best?

COMPARED WITH REGULAR palm oil, high oleic palm oil—including the trademarked fera fruit oil—offers a significant nutritional upgrade.

Traditional palm oil contains about 50 percent saturated fat, including about 40 percent oleic acid, and 10 percent polyunsaturated fatty acids. OxG, the hybrid that produces fera fruit, contains 50 percent oleic acid, 33 percent saturated fatty acids, and 12 percent polyunsaturated fatty acids.

As a dietitian, I can get behind these improvements, but the benefits don't translate to real-world benefits quite as well.

The only way you'll eat fera fruit oil is if you're enjoying pre-made food, most likely fried food, from an establishment using it, as it's not currently available for consumer purchase. And while food fried in fera fruit oil may be slightly nutritionally better than traditional palm oil (which most establishments in the U.S. aren't using anyway), it's still fried food.

This ratio not only contains less saturated fat, but also helps maintain stability over multiple rounds of deep frying compared to other oils. A study presented at the 21st International Oil Palm Conference found that high oleic palm oil lasted more rounds of frying than palm, sunflower, soy, or canola. Because it has less polyunsaturated fat and more monounsaturated and saturated fat, it resists degradation better. This adds up to cost savings, because the oil can be used multiple times, but there's unlikely much of a health advantage. Deep-frying meat and starchy foods in any oil can create harmful compounds, but the link between reusing oil, oil stability, and human health is less clear.

Unrefined high oleic palm oil is rich in antioxidants, including carotenoids and vitamin E. Fera fruit oil is marketed as clean, neutral-tasting, and expeller-pressed, but it offers no guarantee or information on what antioxidants are in the bottle at use or how much.

So while this all sounds great on paper, it's hard to tell how it actually translates into real-world benefits. Is it worth the hype? I'd personally like to see tangible evidence that it does before shelling out extra money for it, and that evidence doesn't seem to exist yet.

Prior to October 15, Erewhon used avocado oil in its fryers. So while there's no arguing that Fera fruit oil has a healthier fatty acid profile than regular palm oil, how does it compare to other fruit oils, like avocado and olive oil, in terms of both health and sustainability?

While olive oil has strong evidence supporting its positive effects on human health, especially heart health, clinical research on the health effects of high-oleic palm oil, like Fera fruit oil, is limited. In one study, 160 participants had either 25 mL of high oleic palm oil or 25 mL of extra virgin olive oil daily for three months. Both groups had similar reductions in total cholesterol and LDL-cholesterol. While these results are promising, the study was small, and more clinical trials are needed to confidently say high oleic palm oil is as beneficial as olive oil.

Avocado oil has a favorable fatty acid profile of 71 percent monounsaturated fatty acids, 13 percent polyunsaturated fatty acids, and 16 percent saturated fatty acids. Fera fruit oil has more saturated fat and less monounsaturated fat, but no head-to-head studies have tested their health effects.

When an elite grocery store like Erewhon switches to a new fryer oil, it's easy to assume it's the healthiest choice. But I wouldn't be so quick to jump on board.

After reviewing the research and understanding the food climate we're currently in, where seed oils are viewed as the culprit of all disease and beef tallow is a cure-all, this honestly seems like just another misguided trend. In the context of reality, when you eat an overall healthy and balanced diet, the occasional fried food, whether it's fried in avocado oil, canola oil, or fera fruit oil, will likely have very little impact on your overall health.

Kelsey Kunik, RDN, is a registered dietician and health writer who covers all-things nutrition for Men's Health and Women's Health.

#4843. Are You Experienced?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

I must achieve internal consistency. —Edmund Husserl, turning an Erlebnis (Type I experience) into an Erfahrung (Type II experience)

The gods decreed that I shall not be a translator, and I am grateful for that. A direct translation from one language to another is a goal we can strive for, but rarely attain fully. The words of any particular language are rich in unique shades of meaning, allusions, emotional undertones, and cross-references to synonyms, which live lives of their own.

Homer called his hero Odysseus πολύτροπος (polytropos), literally “a man of many turns.” But being “of many turns” does not call forth useful associations in English, and so translators have struggled with—and argued with each other about—what to make of polytropos. Some render the idea as “endlessly cunning” (Mitchell, 2014), while others prefer “complicated” (Wilson, 2018). Neither hits the mark. One might as well try shrewd, crafty, clever, or inventive. “Endlessly cunning” is marred by the addition of the adverb, and “complicated” makes it sound like Odysseus needs therapy. “Complex” would have been a better choice. I prefer the phrase “a man of many devices” (Murray, 1919), which recognizes Odysseus’s rich and variable toolbox of survival skills, including those involving deception.

Different languages emphasize and elaborate different concepts, whatever is important in their natural and cultural context. We can marvel at some of these differences. Since Franz Boas (1911) suggested the Greenland Inuit have four different words for snow, others have grown the list, while still others have declared Boas’s observation a myth, one they find vexingly persistent. Other inter-language differences are less controversial, and some of these refer to psychological states. How many types of love are there? The Hebrew tradition counts four. What kinds of longing are there? Is the Portuguese saudade equivalent to the German Sehnsucht? On Seinfeld, Kramer asks George if he has ever yearned. “Yearned?” George replies. “I’ve craved!”

Psychology can be understood as the science of behavior and experience. Both terms carry complexity, and the latter more so than the former. What, we ask, is an experience? It does not take a Ludwig Wittgenstein to see that this concept embraces many variants that may not even share a single common feature. To say that an experience is whatever one experiences is to kick the can down the road; it is a tautology.

When I asked A.I. Claude what an experience is, I received this response: “Experience (noun) has two main senses, and the difference matters.” Claude goes on to explain that one of these senses refers to a process or event, with a first-person involvement. A first kiss delivers this kind of experience. Another sense refers to accumulated knowledge or skill; the sort of thing you put on your résumé. The first sense is what is sometimes called lived experience, whereas the second sense goes further by demanding that something has been learned, something that contributes to the person’s σωφροσύνη (sophrosyne), or practical wisdom. Anyone can have a store of Type I (lived) experiences, but this does not make them “experienced.” The participle must be earned. To have lived experience may simply mean that one hasn’t died yet. To have Type II (empirical) experience means to have made active investments in life that can be cashed out to help reach one’s goals and enhance one’s well-being.

Explaining the conceptual difference between Type I and Type II experience in English requires space, patience, and some circumlocution. The German language offers a clean distinction between Erlebnis, ɛɐˈleːpnɪs, and Erfahrung, ɛɐ̯ˈfaːʁʊŋ. The difference between the two was elaborated by the philosophers Wilhelm Dilthey (1883) and Edmund Husserl (1900-1901), whose work is interesting to consider in light of today’s debates over epistemology (Krueger, 2026). Expressing a popular view, Aziz and Anjum (2025) suggest that the prevailing scientific ethos in psychology is limited and systematically biased by excluding, misrepresenting, and disadvantaging many human populations. What is silenced, according to this view, are the lived experiences existing in these populations. These lived experiences, it is further argued, must be given their due; they must be heard and respected. And so, the argument goes on, these lived experiences must be acknowledged as an alternative epistemology, a way of knowing things, a way of having “knowledges.” Authors arguing the line pursued by Aziz and Anjum differ in how far they wish to go. Some are willing to settle for a lived-experience epistemology being accepted as equivalent to the scientific theory-and-data epistemology. Others wish to see psychological science be remade in light of lived experiences. These writers view the traditional scientific epistemology as oppressive, colonialist, and exploitative.

Dilthey and Husserl would pause here. To them, Erlebnis (Experience Type I) and Erfahrung (Experience Type II) are equally essential to the human condition; they cannot be pitted against each other. What contemporary critics of conventional empirical science seem to miss is that Erlebnis cannot absorb Erfahrung. Being effortful, empirical, and hard-won, Erfahrung is the grounds for reasoned beliefs that can be put to the test, that can be modified or overturned by continued activity. Erfahrung remains a work in progress. An Erlebnis, by contrast, is registered, perhaps committed to memory, and then gradually lost. A tourist has Erlebnisse; a traveler gathers Erfahrungen. It is the difference between perception and cognition.

Science is Erfahrung tamed, structured, and refined into a systematic method. Well-designed studies are efficient ways of learning Nature’s secrets. We can have an Erlebnis when walking into the woods, but only by planting a garden, by experimenting with different seeds, and by pruning excess growth, can we come to have the kind of Erfahrung that allows us to explain things and to teach what we have learned. The rejection of science from the lived-experience perspective is a short-sighted endeavor. The most it can hope to achieve is a narrative. Listening to these narratives can be an Erlebnis, but what can it teach us?

Once the difference between the two types of experience is understood, many familiar narratives appear in a new light. An ancient myth tells us that Adam and Eve had lovely Erlebnisse in the Garden of Eden. In the Land of Nod, they were forced to make Erfahrungen. With that, they became self-aware.

Note: The image above shows what Claude produced when asked to capture the concept of lived experience visually. The effort is interesting but not entirely satisfying since there are several dimensions (time, space, meaning) cross-cutting a scheme built on the idea of concentricity. I confirm that I never use AI to do my writing for me.

Aziz, M. & Anjum G. (2025). Rethinking knowledge systems in psychology: addressing epistemic hegemony and systemic obstacles in climate change studies. Frontiers in Psychology, 16, Article 1533802. doi: 10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1533802.

Boas, F. (1911). Handbook of American Indian Languages, 1. Washington: Government Print Office. Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology, Bulletin 40.

Dilthey, W. (1883). Einleitung in die Geisteswissenschaften: Versuch einer Grundlegung für das Studium der Gesellschaft und der Geschichte [Introduction to the human sciences: An attempt to lay a foundation for the study of society and history] (Vol. 1). Duncker & Humblot.

Husserl, E. (1900–1901). Logische Untersuchungen [Logical investigations] (Vols. 1–2). Max Niemeyer.

Krueger, J. I. (2026). What it means to understand vs explain in psychology. Psychology Today Online. https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/one-among-many/202606/what-it-m…

Mitchell, S. (2014). The Odyssey - Homer. Washington Square Press.

Murray, A. T. (1919). The Odyssey – Homer. Putnam.

Wilson, E. (2018). The Odyssey - Homer. Norton.

The discount doesn’t stack with B&N’s Premium Membership discount, and a few of the most popular new 4K releases are already out of stock online. We checked every price and stock status in this post on Barnes & Noble Wednesday afternoon, November 11.

A family movie night pick that holds up for the grown-ups

Plenty of family movies wear thin for the adults in the room by the fifth viewing, but The Princess Bride keeps getting quoted at dinner tables for a reason. The Criterion edition of The Princess Bride is $24.99 at Barnes & Noble, half of its $49.99 list price. B&N lists it as a 4K Ultra HD and Blu-ray combo, so the standard disc covers any player in the house that can’t handle 4K. Rob Reiner’s 1987 fairy tale is a good place to start if you’re building a disc collection for a family that mostly streams.

The Coens’ Best Picture winner on 4K disc

Javier Bardem’s coin-flipping hitman is one of the scariest villains of the century, and the film around him won Best Picture. The No Country for Old Men 4K Blu-ray is $24.99, down from $49.99. Joel and Ethan Coen’s 2007 West Texas chase also stars Josh Brolin as the hunter who stumbles onto $2 million in drug money and Tommy Lee Jones as the sheriff trying to keep up.

Akira Kurosawa made Yojimbo in 1961 and followed it with Sanjuro a year later, both starring Toshiro Mifune as the same scruffy, sharp-witted ronin. The Yojimbo/Sanjuro 4K Blu-ray set puts both films on 4K for $39.99, which works out to about $20 per movie. If Yojimbo’s plot sounds familiar, that’s because Sergio Leone borrowed it for A Fistful of Dollars. This set pairs well with the Seven Samurai 4K Blu-ray, which is $29.99.

Ten films, 20 discs and more than 25 hours of extras

This is the splurge pick in the sale, but per film it costs about the same as the single 4K discs and adds a Blu-ray copy of each movie. The Wes Anderson Archive: Ten Films, Twenty-Five Years is $249.99, half of its $499.99 list price, which comes to $25 per film. Criterion says the set includes ten 4K UHD discs in Dolby Vision HDR, ten Blu-rays and more than 25 hours of special features, running from Bottle Rocket through The French Dispatch. Every film in the set has new 4K masters supervised and approved by Anderson, according to Criterion.

The Princess Bride, No Country for Old Men and Yojimbo/Sanjuro are covered above. Most of the bestselling single-film 4K discs are $24.99, including Wall-E and David Lynch’s Mulholland Dr. A few older classics, like Citizen Kane, are $29.99. You need a 4K player to watch these discs, and our guide to the best Blu-ray players covers the 4K models worth buying.

The bestselling standard Blu-rays are mostly $19.99, and they play on any Blu-ray player or game console with a disc drive. The KPop Demon Hunters Blu-ray is $19.99 and the KPop Demon Hunters DVD is $14.99, though its 4K edition is out of stock online. Bong Joon-ho’s Parasite is also $19.99.

The Wes Anderson Archive and Yojimbo/Sanjuro are covered above. Box sets get the same 50 percent cut as single discs, and the big director collections are where the dollar savings add up. The 30-disc Ingmar Bergman’s Cinema set is $149.99, and the Essential Fellini set is $124.99.

#4839. A wobbly exoplanet vanished—but astronomers aren’t worried

Published Nov 11, 2026 4:01 PM EST

For the first time, astronomers witnessed a gigantic exoplanet dramatically vanish from view. But the “hot Jupiter” located about 1,000 light-years from Earth didn’t evaporate into the vacuum of space. Instead, the gravitational pull from an uncomfortably close neighbor is causing TOI-2535 b to wobble in its orbit thanks to the same dynamics dictating solar and lunar eclipses. The unusual discovery is detailed in a study recently published in Astrophysical Journal Letters, and relies on observations gathered by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) orbital telescope.

“We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true,” Samuel Yee, a University of California Los Angeles (UCLA) astronomer and study co-author, explained in a recent profile. “If there are multiple planets in a system, they can affect each other’s orbits.”

Astronomers first began examining TOI-2535 b in April 2019 using TESS. The eagle-eyed telescope identifies new planets by flagging subtle changes in stellar brightness. These changes are often caused by a previously unknown planet’s transit in front of its star as seen from Earth. In some ways, TOI-2535 b resembles our solar system’s largest planet, but it is even closer to its own star than Mercury is to our sun. While Mercury takes 88 days to complete the trip, TOI-2535 b circles back around once every 8.25 days.

While using TESS to get glimpses of TOI-2535 b over the next seven years, researchers realized the hot Jupiter’s transits didn’t occur on a regular schedule like most other planets. Instead, the exoplanet’s light fluctuations could arrive upwards of six hours earlier or later than predicted. Over time, astronomers also noticed these transits become shallower and shorter. Then, in March, TOI-2535 b simply didn’t show up during the space telescope’s scan of the system.

Researchers including Yee now believe their hot Jupiter isn’t alone—it actually has an incredibly close gas giant neighbor with a comparatively tilted orbit. The two planets’ relationship causes them to essentially wobble like a pair of tops, eventually throwing one another out of alignment so that they disappear from Earth’s viewpoint.

“This is the most extreme example we’ve seen because the two planets are interacting so strongly,” said Yee. “The planet’s orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching.”

The forces at play are the same as those that ensure eclipses don’t follow a regularly repeating cycle. UCLA astrophysicist and study co-author Erik Petigura explained that this is due to the moon’s tilted orbit, which comes from its cataclysmic early formation following a collision with Earth.

“If the moon’s orbit around the Earth was perfectly aligned with the Earth’s orbit around the sun, we would see an eclipse every month,” Petigura explained.

Yee, Petigura, and their colleagues are lucky to have spotted TOI-2535’s disappearing act when they did. Based on their calculations, its next transit in front of its star won’t occur for another 30 to 50 years—although they may see its partner planet sooner once it emerges from behind its stellar anchor.

#4838. Why Gratitude Sometimes Backfires

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

You can appreciate the people in your life and still dread being asked to announce it over dinner.

The turkey is carved. The cranberry sauce has made its annual appearance in the shape of the can it came from. Then someone says: “Let’s go around the table and say what we’re grateful for.”

Forks pause midair. Eyes drift toward the mashed potatoes like they might offer an escape.

A cousin says something heartfelt and beautiful, and now the emotional bar has been raised to Olympic height.

Am I grateful enough? Should I say something profound?

Gratitude rituals are meant to create warmth. And often they do. But psychologically, gratitude is a little more complicated than the greeting cards suggest.

The benefits are real. A 2023 meta-analysis of 25 randomized controlled trials involving 6,745 participants found that expressing gratitude reliably improved happiness, life satisfaction, and psychological well-being compared with neutral activities.

But that doesn’t tell us everything about how gratitude feels in the moment.

In three experiments, psychologists examined people’s feelings after exercises such as recalling another person’s kindness or writing a gratitude letter they never sent. Alongside feeling moved and uplifted, the gratitude participants tended to report more indebtedness (and sometimes more feelings of guilt) than participants who did a neutral task.

It's like unwrapping a gift and realizing you didn’t bring one.

Gratitude can feel uplifting and slightly uncomfortable at the same time. It can carry a kind of social math: They gave + I received = Now I owe them

That discomfort doesn’t necessarily mean something has gone wrong. Wanting to give something back can be part of caring for a relationship.

But if gratitude can make us feel both good and uncomfortable, what happens when the discomfort arrives from somewhere else entirely?

In a randomized study of 156 undergraduates, participants completed about 12 minutes of gratitude practice, mindful breath awareness, loving-kindness, or a neutral visualization exercise. Those who practiced gratitude did report more positive emotion.

But then researchers introduced a stressor: Participants had to submerge their hand in a bucket of ice-cold water while a researcher in a lab coat stood nearby, observing with the emotional warmth of a marble statue — which is exactly as pleasant as it sounds.

Under that stress, the gratitude group actually became the most emotionally reactive, reporting more negative emotion than any of the other groups. And of the four groups, they were also the least likely to donate time to help others afterward.

Does this mean we should cancel giving thanks? Of course not.

Gratitude strengthens relationships and reinforces others’ kindness. But there's a difference between privately reflecting on gratitude and sharing it.

Privately reflecting on someone's kindness can leave us with an emotional mix: appreciation, plus obligation. Expressing gratitude may not make those complicated feelings disappear. But it can offer something more: connection.

A study of 916 students compared four approaches: writing gratitude letters they never sent, sending personal thank-you texts, posting gratitude publicly on social media, or just tracking daily activities. Participants repeated their assigned activity four times over about a week. Those who sent personal thank-you texts showed the strongest gains in feeling connected to and supported by others.

The takeaway isn't that texting is magical. It's that gratitude may do more to strengthen feelings of being connected and supported when we share it directly with the person we're grateful for rather than keeping it to ourselves.

And it may mean more to that person than we realize. In experiments by Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, people expressing gratitude underestimated how positive recipients would feel and overestimated how awkward they would feel.

The thank-you you’re second-guessing may land more warmly than you expect.

In my book, Micropractice: A Science-Backed Approach for Calm, Clarity, and Joy in 30 Seconds or Less, I explore in greater depth how to practice gratitude without getting caught in feelings of indebtedness, and how to weave more appreciation, connection, and joy into the moments you already have.

This Thanksgiving, when you feel gratitude for someone, try expressing it to them. Here’s a simple trick: Put a “you” in the sentence.

Instead of, “I’m grateful for my family," try, “Mom, you’ve always made people feel at home, even when the turkey’s running late.”

Instead of, “I’m grateful for my friends," try, "Noor, you’re the person I call when life gets messy, and somehow you always have a way of making it lighter.”

One describes what matters to you. The other lets someone know they matter.

Gratitude isn’t just noticing goodness. It’s letting someone know they helped create it.

This Thanksgiving, don’t just count your blessings. Let your blessings know they’re counted.

#4837. SpaceX could announce $1.5 trillion Tesla merger in December: report

Elon Musk’s companies are moving faster than expected on a Tesla-SpaceX combination. A deal could be announced as soon as December, which would make it the largest merger ever, according to Bloomberg.

Tesla holds its annual shareholder meeting on December 3, and the same directors who would sign off on the deal are up for re-election.

According to Bloomberg’s sources, it’s now a negotiation over price and control, with boards and advisers on both sides involved. December is the target, but early 2027 is also on the table.

One of the variables on the table is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive. So, as expected, this is shaping up as SpaceX absorbing Tesla, not the other way around.

That fits the valuations. SpaceX is worth over $1.9 trillion after its June IPO, while Tesla sits around $1.5 trillion. For scale, the record for a single deal has long been Vodafone’s $183 billion takeover of Mannesmann in 2000, and even SpaceX’s roughly $250 billion purchase of xAI (a private company at the time) earlier this year would be dwarfed.

Neither company commented. Tesla stock rose as much as 1.9% on the report.

We’ve been tracking this since May, when Musk first floated merging the two companies weeks before the SpaceX IPO. At the time, we called it the fourth time Musk would make a more than $1 billion self-dealing transaction, after SolarCity, Twitter/X, and Tesla’s $2 billion xAI investment that turned into SpaceX stock.

Then, in October, Tesla’s proxy filing read like a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees, has sat on SpaceX’s board since February. The ballot for the December 3 meeting is limited to re-electing Musk, chair Robyn Denholm, and JB Straubel to terms through 2029, plus a say-on-pay vote and the auditor.

A day later, Musk confirmed that both boards had formed special committees to explore a merger.

The governance piece is where Tesla shareholders should pay the most attention.

Musk owns about 20% of Tesla but controlled roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power through super-voting shares, according to its S-1. Swapping Tesla shares for SpaceX shares means trading one-share-one-vote for a company where Musk’s control is effectively locked in.

And the deal itself pays Musk. Under the change-in-control terms in his 2025 CEO award, the operational milestones drop out and the market cap test runs at the deal price, with earned shares vesting immediately. Based on the share count in the proxy, a deal valuing Tesla at $2 trillion (about a 33% premium to where it trades now) would clear the first market cap tranche on the spot. His 286 million restricted shares from the 2018 package also accelerate on a change in control.

Bloomberg reports that one of the main obstacles is how to ring-fence Tesla’s China business. A JPMorgan analyst described SpaceX’s defense and government work and Tesla’s China footprint as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” for regulators and shareholders.

That’s the same issue behind the Wall Street Journal’s July report that Tesla was weighing a sale or spinoff of its China operations, which Musk denied. Giga Shanghai is Tesla’s most productive factory and builds more than half of its cars. It shipped 67,829 vehicles in October alone.

Politics is the other wild card. Congress flipped to Democrats in the midterms, and they’ve said Musk’s companies and his political ties will get a hard look. Bloomberg previously reported the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

I suspected that the midterms might accelerate the timeline. The Dems don’t take office until January, and Musk likely wants to move this as far along as possible before then.

No rational independent board would offer $1.5 trillion (much less $2 trillion) for Tesla. It is a shrinking EV company with a few fantasy projects that are not delivering. But endlessly diluting other stockholders is his thing.

As for the “independent committees”, those are obviously a joke. No one believes that, but it’s not like Tesla’s shareholders would care at this point. Tesla’s stock has been a dud for 4 years, and shareholders’ best chance to see a return is another self-deal with Musk.

Tesla is a car and energy company with falling car sales, and it would get folded into a rocket, satellite, and AI company that’s valued at a premium to it and controlled by one person.

This is the end game. At least, it looks like Elon is running out of companies to fold together to hide underperformance.

#4836. Volunteer to play the ‘bad guy’ for the TSA’s bomb-sniffing dogs

Published Nov 11, 2026 4:36 PM EST

Want to play with dogs at the airport and have it be for a good cause? Well, boy, do we have the volunteer gig for you. It’s actually less playtime and more very serious Transportation Security Administration (TSA) work, but there’s still dogs, so we consider that a win: The TSA is currently looking for volunteers to be explosive detection K9 decoys, and honestly there may not be a cuter way to spend a weekend. Let these very smart dogs show us all just how smart they really are!

In their call for volunteers, the TSA says that a volunteer shift with these crafty canines “may feel like a high-stakes game of hide and seek.” They also emphasize that “this training is a serious and important part of keeping our canine teams ready for duty.”

You’re basically pretending to be an airport bad guy or, as the TSA puts it, “a covert role player.” You might be tasked with carrying a “training item” and wander around an airport acting like you’re just an everyday passenger in the ticketing lobbies, going through security, or just generally waiting around for their boarding time. Then, the real game begins, and the canine team will try to sniff you out.

The entire set-up is meant to mimic what these dogs might face in the real world.

The entire volunteer shift takes about two to three hours.

There aren’t a ton of restrictions on who can volunteer with these very smart doggies. You have to be at least 18 years old to volunteer. Although minors can volunteer alongside an adult companion, they can only participate in limited ways.

You also have to be comfortable sitting, walking, and moving around an airport. However, wheelchair and scooter users can participate in the program.

You can check out their annual calendar, which will be available in November or December. A German shorthaired pointer named Bolt won the TSA’S Cutest Canine Contest for 2026 and will be one of the working dogs featured on the 2027 calendar.
